title: Headline Analyzer: how it works, formula and examples
excerpt: Headline Analyzer: Score a headline — length, word balance, emotion and power words. Learn how to use it, the formula behind it, a worked example and answers…
content:
The [Headline Analyzer](/headline-analyzer) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Score a headline — length, word balance, emotion and power words. Enter your headline and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Score a headline the way a headline tool does: length, word count, and the balance of common, uncommon, emotional and power words — the mix that makes people click. A strong headline is 6–12 words and 40–70 characters, with 20–30% common words, 10–20% uncommon words, 10–15% emotional words and at least one power word. The score is a writing guide, not a ranking promise: a great headline still needs a great page behind it. Everything runs in your browser.

## How to use the Headline Analyzer

Start by typing or pasting your headline. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause. The steps below walk through each input in order.

1. Type or paste your headline.
2. Read the score and the checks below it.
3. Adjust the wording — add a number, a power word or an emotional word — and watch the score move.

## Formula

Score out of 100: 25 points for 6–12 words, 15 for 40–70 characters, 15 each for common, uncommon and emotional word balance, 10 for a power word and 5 for a number.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Headline Analyzer](/headline-analyzer) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. “7 Proven Ways to Save Money on Your Weekly Groceries” scores well: 9 words, a number, the power word “proven” and the emotional pull of saving money. Try the same figures in the [Headline Analyzer](/headline-analyzer) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Headline: 7 Proven Ways to Save Money on Your Weekly Groceries), the [Headline Analyzer](/headline-analyzer) returns Headline score: 85 / 100 (Strong), Words: 10, Characters: 52, Common words: 30%, Uncommon words: 10%, Emotional words: 0%, Power words: 3, Contains a number: Yes. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Website SEO Audit](/website-seo-audit) is worth a look before you finish.

## What the score measures

Six things: word count (6–12 is best), character length (40–70, so the headline fits in search results), common words (20–30%, for readability), uncommon words (10–20%, to catch the eye), emotional words (10–15%, to make people care) and power words (at least one — proven, free, secret, ultimate). A number and a question each help too.

## What the score does not measure

Whether the headline is true, whether it matches the page, or whether anyone will actually click it. A headline that promises what the page does not deliver earns bounces, not readers. Use the score to sharpen an honest headline, not to dress up a weak page.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Start with a number — list headlines get more clicks.
- One power word (proven, secret, free, ultimate) adds punch.
- Keep it under 70 characters so it is not cut off in search results.

## Frequently asked questions

### What makes a good headline?

Six to twelve words, 40–70 characters, a mix of common words for readability, uncommon and emotional words for attention, and at least one power word. A number helps too. Try it with your own numbers in the [Headline Analyzer](/headline-analyzer) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Does a high headline score guarantee clicks?

No. It measures the headline's structure against what tends to work. The page behind it still has to deliver on the promise. Try it with your own numbers in the [Headline Analyzer](/headline-analyzer) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### How long should a headline be?

Aim for 6–12 words and 40–70 characters — long enough to say something specific, short enough to fit in search results. Try it with your own numbers in the [Headline Analyzer](/headline-analyzer) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What formula does the Headline Analyzer use?

Score out of 100: 25 points for 6–12 words, 15 for 40–70 characters, 15 each for common, uncommon and emotional word balance, 10 for a power word and 5 for a number. You can see it in action in the [Headline Analyzer](/headline-analyzer) — enter your own values and the result updates as you type.
